Eyherabide, Rokem, Herz & Samengo (2008) on CRCNS ia-1¶

Paper: H. G. Eyherabide, A. Rokem, A. V. M. Herz and I. Samengo (2008), "Burst firing is a neural code in an insect auditory system", Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience, doi:10.3389/neuro.10.003.2008. The claims file (claims/crcns-ia-1/10.3389-neuro.10.003.2008.yaml) was written from the version of record in PubMed Central (PMC2525941), with its Methods and the legends of Figures 1 to 10 and Table 1; the paper has no supplement and links no code.

Dataset: CRCNS data set ia-1, doi:10.6080/K0BG2KWB, read from the public bucket crcnsarchive (ia-1/crcns-ia1.zip), streamed and opened in place.

Version: CRCNS data sets are not versioned, so the version is recorded as unversioned and the file read is pinned by its MD5 sum in the data set's checksums.md5: crcns-ia1.zip f0740514fabc6995fe54b2a361b6c763 (the helper checks the object's ETag against it before reading; the object was last modified 2026-02-11). This is the only published state of the data set, so it is the one pinned. Only Data1 is used: the data descriptor names it as the data of this paper; Data2 (2004) is unpublished and used other stimuli.

Two analyses draw random numbers, the shifted-onset baseline of Figure 7 and the size-matched control of sigma-n-below-sta-sigma; each has its own seeded generator.

Revised after the first verification round. The main population is now selection (c), which also leaves out sessions with fewer than 98 trials and sessions sorted off-line (see "Session selection"); the first round's population, selection (a), is shown beside it. The central maximum of the burst-triggered averages is searched before the burst onset; a first-peak reading with the refractory plateau left out, a shifted-onset baseline for the information measures, a size-matched control for sigma_n, sensitivity to the minimum number of bursts, and checks of the trial blocks and of the firing_rates file were added.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

import ia1

pd.set_option("display.width", 200)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 40)
pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 200)

z = ia1.open_zip()
sessions = ia1.load_sessions(z)
cells = ia1.load_singlecells(z)
shapes = {name: ia1.load_stimulus_shape(z, name) for name in sorted({s.stimulus for s in sessions})}
cell_of = {e: i for i, row in enumerate(cells) for e in row}

Data check¶

What was loaded, and the checks of the description against the values. The data descriptor says: spike times in microseconds from the stimulus trigger; trials of the first 1000 ms of the stimulus, 98 to 533 per stimulus; 700 ms pauses; two interleaved stimuli per experiment; cell.dat gives the stimulus names and intensities (the maximal intensity, mean plus 3 SD); stimulus files at 20 kHz, 10 s long; singlecells.txt lists the experiments made on one cell.

# Trial blocks: spikes after the 1 s stimulus fall in the pause. A block holding two trials (a

Trial blocks. Spikes reach 2.76 s, later than one trial and its pause, so a block without a header could hold two trials. The check above shows that late spikes occur only in off-line sorted sessions, at the low rate of the pause, and that no block restarts its times or holds twice the spike count of the others: each block is one trial and the trial counts stand (the data set's own firing_rates file gives the same counts in 136 of 138 files). The firing_rates file is not a selection: its +/- value is far above any trial-to-trial SD of the rate.

The stimulus files are named for their SD and cutoff (gauss_st6_co200 is SD 6 dB, cutoff 200 Hz). Their SDs over the first second can be checked against the names (6 dB files near 6 dB).

Clock check. Spikes and stimuli share the trial's clock if the spike-triggered average of the stimulus (STA) shows the upstroke a few ms before the spike, which the paper describes (Figure 1: "responses typically appear after stimulus upstrokes with an delay of 3.4 msec"). The contrast is the same STA computed from the stimulus shifted by 100 ms, which keeps every property of the stimulus and the spike train except their alignment.

P = [s for s in sessions if s.protocol]          # sessions in the paper's seven protocols


def stim_db(s):
    return shapes[s.stimulus] + s.intensity


def spikes_in(s, t0=ia1.T0, t1=ia1.T1):
    return np.concatenate([t[(t >= t0) & (t < t1)] for t in s.trials])


rows = []
for s in P:
    st = stim_db(s)
    sp = spikes_in(s)
    seg, tt = ia1.segments(st, sp)
    sta = seg.mean(0) - st[4000:20000].mean()
    seg2, _ = ia1.segments(st, sp - 0.1)
    sta2 = seg2.mean(0) - st[4000:20000].mean()
    rows.append(dict(session=s.name, protocol=s.protocol, sta_peak=sta.max(), lat_ms=-tt[np.argmax(sta[tt <= 0])] * 1e3,
                     shifted_peak=sta2.max()))
C = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print("STA peak above the mean stimulus (dB): median", round(C.sta_peak.median(), 2), " range", round(C.sta_peak.min(), 2), "to", round(C.sta_peak.max(), 2))
print("with the stimulus shifted by 100 ms: median", round(C.shifted_peak.median(), 2), " range", round(C.shifted_peak.min(), 2), "to", round(C.shifted_peak.max(), 2))
print("sessions whose STA peak exceeds the shifted one:", (C.sta_peak > C.shifted_peak).sum(), "of", len(C))
print("latency of the STA maximum (ms): median", C.lat_ms.median(), " range", C.lat_ms.min(), "to", C.lat_ms.max())
print("sessions where the true STA peak is under 1 dB:", list(C.session[C.sta_peak < 1]))
print("sessions whose STA maximum is at the spike (latency 0 ms, the edge of the search):", list(C.session[C.lat_ms <= 0]))

Session selection and burst identification¶

Kept sessions (claim data-sessions-and-trials). The paper keeps sessions whose trial-to-trial SD of the firing rate is below 35 Hz and whose mean rate is about 100 Hz. Readings, from the criterion: (a) the SD condition alone; (b) the SD condition and a target rate of 100 Hz where the header records one. Per-trial rates over 200 to 1000 ms, and over the whole 1 s as a variant. Only sessions of the paper's seven protocols (Table 1) can be kept; the data set's other stimuli (gaussModality_co200, lmd_co200, cutoffs 50 and 1600 Hz) are not in the paper's design (Methods: "The other signal could be one of six different stimulation protocols").

Readings (a) and (b) keep 115 and 113 of the 116 seven-protocol sessions, against the paper's 86, so the paper removed sessions by a rule it does not state. Reading (c), added after the first verification, is the SD condition and two exclusions the data suggest: sessions with fewer than 98 trials (the Methods give "N ranging between 98 and 503" for the paper's sessions, so a session with fewer was not among them) and sessions whose spikes were detected off-line (OFFOEL header; the data descriptor says off-line detection was done where the on-line detection "was deemed to be inexact"). The off-line exclusion has no passage in the paper behind it; it is taken because, with it, the kept sessions per protocol and the bursting sessions per protocol come close to Table 1 (below). Because it was chosen in part from the counts of Table 1, it does not decide data-sessions-and-trials, table1-sessions-per-protocol or table1-bursting-sessions, where it is shown as a variant. For the other claims it is the main population, an assumption; the results over the 115 sessions of reading (a) are shown beside it.

Bursts, by the Methods (Burst identification), under every combination of the readings of the open details (claims file, opening comment): peak (a) first local maximum, (b) largest value in 0 < tau < 5 ms, and (c) the first local maximum after C_s first rises significantly above its refractory plateau (added after the first verification, see ia1.py); minimum (a) first significant local minimum after the peak, (b) lowest value up to 1.25 / cutoff; error bar N (a) the number of product terms, (b) the number of trials, and (c) sigma the SD over trials of each trial's C_s with N the number of trials (added here, see ia1.py).

def kept(reading="a", window="200-1000"):
    col = "rate_sd" if window == "200-1000" else "rate_sd_full"
    out = []
    for s in P:
        row = D.loc[D.session == s.name].iloc[0]
        ok = row[col] < 35
        if reading == "b" and not np.isnan(row.desired_rate):
            ok = ok and row.desired_rate == 100
        if reading == "c":
            ok = ok and not s.offline and s.n_trials >= 98
        if ok:
            out.append(s)
    return out


T1_SESS = [43, 6, 7, 7, 8, 7, 8]
sv = D[D.protocol.notna() & (D.rate_sd < 35)]
rows = []
for label, g in [("SD < 35 Hz (reading a)", sv), ("  without off-line sorted sessions", sv[~sv.offline]),
                 ("  without sessions under 98 trials", sv[sv.n_trials >= 98]),
                 ("  without both (reading c)", sv[~sv.offline & (sv.n_trials >= 98)]),
                 ("  without the 450 ms pause sessions", sv[sv.pause_ms != 450]),
                 ("  without off-line and 450 ms pause", sv[~sv.offline & (sv.pause_ms != 450)]),
                 ("  without off-line, 450 ms pause and under 98 trials", sv[~sv.offline & (sv.pause_ms != 450) & (sv.n_trials >= 98)])]:
    v = [int((g.protocol == p).sum()) for p in range(1, 8)]
    rows.append(dict(selection=label, sessions=len(g), **{f"p{p}": x for p, x in zip(range(1, 8), v)},
                     within_10pct=sum(abs(x - e) <= 0.1 * e for x, e in zip(v, T1_SESS)),
                     min_trials=g.n_trials.min(), mean_trials=round(g.n_trials.mean(), 1)))
rows.append(dict(selection="paper (Table 1)", sessions=86, **{f"p{p}": x for p, x in zip(range(1, 8), T1_SESS)}))
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
print("off-line sorted seven-protocol sessions by protocol:", sv[sv.offline].protocol.value_counts().sort_index().to_dict(),
      "; sessions under 98 trials:", sv.loc[sv.n_trials < 98, ["session", "n_trials", "offline"]].values.tolist())

KEPT = kept("c")
KEPT_A = kept("a")
POP = {"c": {s.name for s in KEPT}, "a": {s.name for s in KEPT_A}}
COMBOS = list(itertools.product("abc", "ab", "abc"))
MAIN = ("b", "a", "a")
limits = {c: {s.name: ia1.burst_limit(s.trials, s.cutoff, *c)[0] for s in P} for c in COMBOS}
for c in COMBOS:
    lim = limits[c]
    nb = sum(lim[s.name] > 0 for s in KEPT)
    na = sum(lim[s.name] > 0 for s in KEPT_A)
    print("peak %s, minimum %s, N %s: bursting %3d of %d kept (c), %3d of %d (a); median limiting ISI %s ms" % (
        *c, nb, len(KEPT), na, len(KEPT_A), np.round(np.median([lim[s.name] for s in KEPT if lim[s.name] > 0]) * 1e3, 2) if nb else "-"))
LIM = limits[MAIN]

data-sessions-and-trials¶

Thirty-seven receptor cells were recorded from 23 animals, giving 132 sessions, of which 86 met the firing-rate and stationarity conditions; each stimulus was repeated 98 to 503 times, 172 on average.

Data1 does not record the animal. The recording date is shown as a stand-in (one animal per day is an assumption the descriptor does not make); cells are the rows of singlecells.txt.

In [5]:
def describe(sel, label):
    names = {s.name for s in sel}
    d = D[D.session.isin(names)]
    # cells: rows of singlecells.txt, plus each experiment it does not list
    return dict(population=label, cells=d.cell[d.cell >= 0].nunique() + d.exp[d.cell < 0].nunique(),
                dates=d.date.nunique(), sessions=len(d), min_trials=d.n_trials.min(), max_trials=d.n_trials.max(),
                mean_trials=round(d.n_trials.mean(), 1), mean_rate_sd=round(d.rate_sd.mean(), 2),
                mean_rate_sd_full=round(d.rate_sd_full.mean(), 2))

expected (value, tolerance): {'cells': (37, 3.7), 'sessions_recorded': (132, 13.2), 'kept': (86, 8.6), 'min_trials': (98, 9.8), 'max_trials': (503, 50.3), 'mean_trials': (172, 17.2), 'mean_rate_sd': (6, 0.6)}

Result: partially reproduced. The 116 sessions of the seven protocols come from 37 cells recorded on 23 dates, the paper's 37 cells and 23 animals (if one animal was recorded per date, an assumption, as Data1 does not record the animal). The 122 Gaussian AM sessions (any cutoff) are within 10% of the paper's 132 sessions; all 150 Data1 sessions are not. Under the criterion's readings the selection does not reproduce: the SD < 35 Hz condition keeps 115 of the 116 sessions (113 with the 100 Hz target of reading (b)), against 86, and over them the trials range from 69 (outside 98 +/- 9.8) to 503 and average 160.3 (within 172 +/- 17.2), with a mean trial-to-trial SD of the rate of 6.48 Hz (within 6 +/- 0.6). Reading (c), which also leaves out the sessions with fewer than 98 trials and those sorted off-line, keeps 89 sessions with 98 to 503 trials (mean 168.7) and a mean SD of 6.00 Hz, within tolerance, but they come from 29 cells recorded on 18 dates, outside 37 +/- 3.7 and 23 +/- 2.3; the 37 cells and 23 dates hold only when counted over all seven-protocol sessions. It adds two exclusions the paper does not give as conditions, chosen in part from these counts (its fewest trials are 98 by construction), so it does not decide this claim; it is used as the population of the claims that follow.

table1-sessions-per-protocol¶

The 86 kept sessions divide among the seven stimulus protocols as 43 (6 dB, 200 Hz), 6 (3 dB, 200 Hz), 7 (12 dB, 200 Hz), 7 (6 dB, 25 Hz), 8 (6 dB, 100 Hz), 7 (6 dB, 400 Hz) and 8 (6 dB, 800 Hz).

In [6]:

Result: not reproduced. None of the seven counts is within 10% of Table 1 under the criterion's readings: the kept sessions are 60, 9, 8, 10, 11, 8 and 9 per protocol (reading (a), 200 to 1000 ms) against 43, 6, 7, 7, 8, 7 and 8. Under reading (c) of the selection they are 47, 6, 7, 7, 8, 7 and 7, six of seven within tolerance (800 Hz has 7 against 8), but that reading was chosen in part from these counts. The data set holds every reference session paired with each other protocol (55 experiments) and more reference sessions than the paper counts.

firing-rate-uniform¶

The kept sessions had a mean firing rate of 113 Hz (SD 16 Hz) that did not differ significantly across stimulus conditions (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.58).

In [7]:
rows = []
for label, sel, col in [("kept (c), 200-1000 ms", kept("c"), "rate"), ("kept (c), 0-1000 ms", kept("c", "full"), "rate_full"),
                        ("kept (a), 200-1000 ms", kept("a"), "rate"), ("kept (a), 0-1000 ms", kept("a", "full"), "rate_full"),
                        ("all seven-protocol sessions, 200-1000 ms", P, "rate"), ("all seven-protocol sessions, 0-1000 ms", P, "rate_full"),
                        ("kept (b), 200-1000 ms", kept("b"), "rate")]:
    d = D[D.session.isin({s.name for s in sel})]
    groups = [g[col].values for _, g in d.groupby("protocol")]
    F, p = stats.f_oneway(*groups)
    rows.append(dict(population=label, n=len(d), mean_rate=round(d[col].mean(), 1), sd_rate=round(d[col].std(ddof=1), 1),
                     F=round(F, 2), p=round(p, 3)))
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

mean rate by protocol (kept (c), 200-1000 ms): {1.0: 107.5, 2.0: 115.3, 3.0: 104.8, 4.0: 102.4, 5.0: 104.9, 6.0: 107.3, 7.0: 107.2}

Result: reproduced. Over the 89 sessions of selection (c) the mean rate is 107.1 Hz (within 113 +/- 16) with SD 14.5 Hz (within 16 +/- 1.6), and a one-way ANOVA across the seven protocols finds no difference (F = 0.49, p = 0.814). Over the 115 sessions of selection (a) the mean is 110.2 Hz (SD 16.7), F = 0.49, p = 0.818; over all seven-protocol sessions and with whole-trial rates the ANOVA gives p between 0.471 and 0.809. No population shows a significant difference.

threshold-population (blocked)¶

The mean threshold of the cells at their best frequency was 58 dB (SD 14 dB).

Data1 holds spike times, cell.dat (stimulus names and the intensities they were played at) and the stimuli. It holds no threshold, best-frequency or tuning (f-I) measurement: the listing below shows every kind of file in Data1. Blocked, data_missing.

table1-bursting-sessions¶

The number of sessions with bursts of n > 1 depends on the stimulus, from none for 3 dB and for 800 Hz to all 7 for 12 dB and 7 of 8 for 100 Hz; 40 of 43 reference sessions, 6 of 7 at 25 Hz and 3 of 7 at 400 Hz.

Counted over the kept sessions, under every combination of the burst-identification readings. The fraction of sessions is shown beside the counts, since the counts depend on how many sessions are kept.

In [9]:
T1_BURST = [40, 0, 7, 6, 7, 3, 0]
tol = [max(0.1 * e, 0) for e in T1_BURST]


def n_gt1_sessions(sel, lim):
    cnt = collections.Counter()
    for s in sel:
        if lim[s.name] > 0 and (ia1.burst_counts(s.trials, lim[s.name])[1:] > 0).any():
            cnt[s.protocol] += 1
    return [cnt[p] for p in range(1, 8)]


rows = []
for kr in ["c", "a", "b"]:
    sel = kept(kr)
    tot = collections.Counter(s.protocol for s in sel)
    for c in COMBOS:
        v = n_gt1_sessions(sel, limits[c])
        rows.append(dict(kept=kr, readings="".join(c), **{f"p{p}": f"{x}/{tot[p]}" for p, x in zip(range(1, 8), v)},
                         within=sum(abs(x - e) <= t for x, e, t in zip(v, T1_BURST, tol))))
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
print("paper:", [f"{a}/{b}" for a, b in zip(T1_BURST, T1_SESS)])

Result: not reproduced. Under every selection the criterion supports, at most 2 of the 7 counts are within tolerance: over the 115 sessions of selection (a) the main burst reading (peak b, minimum a, N a) gives 52/60, 2/9, 8/8, 9/10, 10/11, 3/8 and 0/9 against 40/43, 0/6, 7/7, 6/7, 7/8, 3/7 and 0/8, and selection (b) gives 2 of 7 as well. Over selection (c) the main reading gives 40/47, 1/6, 7/7, 6/7, 7/8, 3/7 and 0/7, six of seven equal to the paper's, and the first local maximum read with the refractory plateau left out (peak c) gives 37/47 reference sessions and the same other counts. Selection (c) leaves out the off-line sorted sessions, which no passage of the paper supports, and was chosen in part because these counts then come close to Table 1, so it is a variant here and does not decide the outcome. The outcome recorded after the first verification, partially reproduced, rested on selection (c); the second verification found this circular, and the third verification agreed with the change to not reproduced. Under peak reading (a) 5 of 47 reference sessions burst, and with N the number of trials (b) none does.

table1-isolated-spikes¶

The percentage of isolated spikes among all bursts of the bursting sessions depends on the stimulus (74, 100, 62, 60, 55, 96 and 100% for protocols 1 to 7), and in every protocol isolated spikes are the most probable burst.

In [10]:
T1_ISO = [74, 100, 62, 60, 55, 96, 100]


def protocol_counts(sel, lim):
    # Pooled n counts per protocol over the bursting sessions (all sessions where a protocol has none).
    out = {}
    for p in range(1, 8):
        ses = [s for s in sel if s.protocol == p]
        bur = [s for s in ses if lim[s.name] > 0]
        use = bur if bur else ses
        tot = np.zeros(400)
        per = []
        for s in use:
            c = ia1.burst_counts(s.trials, lim[s.name])
            tot[:len(c)] += c
            per.append(c[0] / c.sum())
        out[p] = (np.trim_zeros(tot, "b"), per, len(bur))
    return out


rows = []
PC = {}
for kr, sel, c in [("c", KEPT, c) for c in COMBOS] + [("a", KEPT_A, c) for c in COMBOS]:
    pc = protocol_counts(sel, limits[c])
    PC[(kr, c)] = pc
    iso = [100 * pc[p][0][0] / pc[p][0].sum() for p in range(1, 8)]
    iso_avg = [100 * np.mean(pc[p][1]) for p in range(1, 8)]
    most = [int(np.argmax(pc[p][0]) + 1) for p in range(1, 8)]
    rows.append(dict(kept=kr, readings="".join(c), **{f"p{p}": round(v, 1) for p, v in zip(range(1, 8), iso)},
                     within=sum(abs(v - e) <= 0.1 * e for v, e in zip(iso, T1_ISO)), most_probable_n=most,
                     session_average=[round(v, 1) for v in iso_avg]))
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
print("paper:", T1_ISO)

Result: not reproduced. Under the main reading the pooled percentage of isolated spikes over selection (c) is 80.7, 71.7, 66.1, 78.0, 71.3, 95.0 and 100% against 74, 100, 62, 60, 55, 96 and 100%: 4 of 7 within tolerance (protocols 1, 3, 6, 7). At 3 dB the one bursting session gives 71.7% where the paper has no bursts, and 25 Hz and 100 Hz have more isolated spikes than the paper. No combination of readings brings more than 5 of 7 within tolerance (4 over selection (a)). n = 1 is the most probable burst in every protocol under the main reading, as the paper says. The criterion requires every value; 4 of 7 is below the five of seven at which the other Table 1 criteria call a result partial, so the outcome is not reproduced (the first round recorded it as partially reproduced).

table1-burst-length¶

The highest n and the average n depend on the stimulus; the longest bursts (up to 15 spikes, average 2.10 with SD 3.67) occur at 25 Hz, and no bursts occur at 3 dB or at 800 Hz.

Under the main reading over selection (c) 8 of the 19 values are within tolerance (highest n 7, 9, 8, 14, 7, 5, 1 against 9, 1, 8, 15, 9, 3, 1; average n 1.23, 1.39, 1.49, 1.90, 1.39, 1.05, 1.00 against 1.3, 1, 1.5, 2.1, 1.7, 1.04, 1), below the 10 the criterion needs for a partial reproduction, and no combination of readings under either selection gives more than 9 (peak reading c). The longest bursts are at 25 Hz (14 spikes) and 800 Hz has none, as in the paper, but 3 dB has bursts of up to 9 spikes in its one bursting session.

fig5-burst-probability-vs-stimulus¶

The probability of generating isolated spikes is lowest, and high-n bursts most frequent, for large amplitude fluctuations (12 dB) and cutoff frequencies around 100 Hz.

In [12]:
def pn_table(sel, lim, bursting_only):
    rows = []
    for s in sel:
        if bursting_only and lim[s.name] <= 0:
            continue
        c = ia1.burst_counts(s.trials, lim[s.name]).astype(float)
        c = np.r_[c, np.zeros(3)][:3] / c.sum()
        rows.append(dict(protocol=s.protocol, P1=c[0], P2=c[1], P3=c[2]))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby("protocol").agg(["mean", "std", "size"])


for kr, sel, c in [("c", KEPT, MAIN), ("c", KEPT, ("b", "b", "a")), ("c", KEPT, ("b", "a", "c")), ("c", KEPT, ("a", "a", "a")),
                  ("c", KEPT, ("c", "a", "a")), ("a", KEPT_A, MAIN)]:
    for reading, bo in [("(a) all kept", False), ("(b) bursting only", True)]:
        t = pn_table(sel, limits[c], bo)
        means = t.xs("mean", axis=1, level=1)
        cut = {25: 4, 100: 5, 200: 1, 400: 6, 800: 7}
        sdp = {3: 2, 6: 1, 12: 3}
        p1c = {k: means.P1.get(v, np.nan) for k, v in cut.items()}
        p1s = {k: means.P1.get(v, np.nan) for k, v in sdp.items()}
        print(f"kept ({kr}), readings {''.join(c)}, sessions {reading}")
        print("  P(n=1) by cutoff:", {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in p1c.items()}, " lowest at", min(p1c, key=p1c.get), "Hz")
        print("  P(n=1) by SD:", {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in p1s.items()}, " lowest at", min(p1s, key=p1s.get), "dB")
        for col in ["P2", "P3"]:
            print(f"  {col} by cutoff:", {k: round(means[col].get(v, np.nan), 3) for k, v in cut.items()},
                  " by SD:", {k: round(means[col].get(v, np.nan), 3) for k, v in sdp.items()})
t = pn_table(KEPT, LIM, False)
print("\nmain reading, all kept (c): mean, SD and number of sessions per protocol")
print(t.round(3).to_string())

fig3-correlation-shape¶

For a cell tested with all stimuli, larger stimulus SD gives correlation functions with sharper peaks, and faster stimuli lead from multi-modal (25 Hz) to single-peaked (100, 200 Hz) to shallower and broader correlation functions (400, 800 Hz).

singlecells.txt lists one cell recorded in seven experiments, 03-04-23-ad to -aj, which together hold all seven protocols (six reference sessions, one of each other protocol): this is taken as the cell of Figure 3. C_s is normalised by the squared mean rate so that sessions compare. "Sharper" is read as (a) a higher first peak over the baseline (the mean of C_s/rbar^2 over 20 to 40 ms) and (b) a narrower first peak (full width at half height above that baseline). Peaks are counted on C_s/rbar^2 smoothed with a 1 ms running mean (a standard choice that keeps the ms-scale shape), as local maxima within 0 < tau <= 1.25 / cutoff that rise above the neighbouring minima by more than a prominence threshold; the threshold is not in the paper, so 0.05, 0.1 and 0.2 are shown.

In [13]:
from scipy.signal import find_peaks

fig3_cell = next(row for row in cells if "03-04-23-ad" in row)
F3 = [s for s in P if s.exp in fig3_cell]
rows = []
curves = []
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
for s in F3:
    tau, c, sd, count, ntr, sdt = ia1.correlation(s.trials, 0.06)
    rb = ia1.binned(s.trials).astype(bool).mean() / ia1.DT
    cn = c / rb ** 2
    base = cn[(tau >= 0.02) & (tau <= 0.04)].mean()
    sm = np.convolve(cn, np.ones(10) / 10, mode="same")
    sm[:6] = cn[:6]
    lim_i = int(1.25 / s.cutoff / ia1.DT)
    ip = 1 + np.argmax(cn[1:51])
    height = cn[ip] - base
    width = ia1.fwhm(cn, ip, base) * ia1.DT * 1e3
    npk = {}
    for prom in [0.05, 0.1, 0.2]:
        pk, _ = find_peaks(sm[1:lim_i + 1], prominence=prom)
        npk[prom] = len(pk)
    rows.append(dict(session=s.name, sd=s.sd_cut[0], cutoff=s.cutoff, bursting=LIM[s.name] > 0,
                     limit_ms=round(LIM[s.name] * 1e3, 1), peak_ms=round(tau[ip] * 1e3, 1), peak_height=round(height, 2),
                     peak_fwhm_ms=round(width, 1), **{f"peaks_prom{k}": v for k, v in npk.items()}))
    curves.append(cn[1:])
    ax = axes[0] if s.sd_cut[1] == 200 else axes[1]
    ax.plot(tau[1:] * 1e3, cn[1:], lw=0.8, label=f"{s.sd_cut[0]} dB, {s.cutoff} Hz ({s.exp[-2:]})")

allc = np.concatenate(curves)

Result: reproduced (resting on the peak-counting threshold). In the cell recorded with all seven protocols (03-04-23-ad to -aj) the first peak of C_s/rbar^2 rises above its baseline by 0.50 at 3 dB, 1.14 to 2.35 in the six 6 dB sessions and 5.06 at 12 dB, so it sharpens with SD under reading (a); its width (b) does not order (0.4, 0.4 to 0.5, 0.3 ms). At 25 Hz C_s has 4 to 14 peaks, at 200 Hz one; at 100 Hz one peak at prominence 0.2 and two at 0.05 and 0.1. The 3 dB, 400 Hz and 800 Hz sessions have no separable first peak, as the paper names for Figures 3A, E and F.

method-correlation-error¶

The temporal average of the estimated error of the correlation function was on average 3.4% (SD 1.5%) of the span of C_s.

Delta = sigma / sqrt(N) at each tau, averaged over tau, over max minus min of C_s, averaged over kept sessions. Readings: sigma and N (a), (b) and (c); tau range (a) 0 to 1.25 / cutoff, (b) the whole range up to 800 ms. Whether tau = 0, where C_s holds the self term (rbar / dt, two orders of magnitude above the rest), enters the span is not stated: both are shown.

model-matches-classification (blocked)¶

A threshold-linear Poisson model with refractoriness and no free parameters classifies sessions as bursting or not in agreement with the real data in 86% of sessions, and where both are bursting their limiting ISIs differ by less than 1 ms in 81% of cases.

The model thresholds the stimulus at the cell's measured threshold s_TH before filtering (Eq. 2), and the criterion says the claim is not testable as the paper ran it if the data set does not hold s_TH. Data1 holds no threshold (see threshold-population). Blocked, data_missing; the dependent model-reproduces-coding-trends is blocked for the same reason.

fig6-bursts-less-correlated¶

Representing the spike train as n-bursts reduces correlations between time bins; the mean squared Pearson coefficient over t from 200 to 990 ms and tau from 0 to 10 ms is 2.89 times larger (SD 1.49) for spikes than for bursts, on average over the bursting sessions.

Eq. 11 across trials at each (t, tau). Bin width (a) 0.1 ms, (b) 0.4 ms; tau = 0 included or not. The spike variable is 1 when the bin holds a spike. Bursting sessions under the main burst reading; detail (4) reading (b) (bursting sessions that have bursts of n > 1) is shown too.

Information per burst (Figure 7): per-session measures¶

For every kept session, under the main burst reading, with the bin widths (a) 0.1 ms and (b) 0.4 ms: rbar_n, I_n(1) in bits per event (reading i; reading ii is T = 0.8 s times it), I'_n in bits/s, and the jitter of each n (readings (a) and (b) of the events). Fits are over the n values present. Sessions of reading (a) of the selection are computed and summarised under both selections.

The plug-in estimate of I_n(1) is biased upwards for rare events, and more so the rarer they are, so part of a rise of I_n(1) with n can come from the fall in occurrence. As a baseline (not in the paper), the same measures are computed after shifting each trial's burst onsets by a random offset, wrapped within 200 to 1000 ms (ia1.circular_shift), which keeps the bursts of each trial and removes their locking to the stimulus; ten shifts per session, averaged.

In [16]:
T = ia1.T1 - ia1.T0
rng7 = np.random.default_rng(2008)
info, info_sh = {}, {}
for s in KEPT_A:
    tr, on, n = ia1.bursts(s.trials, LIM[s.name])
    shifted = [ia1.circular_shift(tr, on, s.n_trials, rng7) for _ in range(10)]
    for bw in [1e-4, 4e-4]:
        info[(s.name, bw)] = ia1.information(ia1.rates_of(on, n, s.n_trials, bw))
        sh = [ia1.information(ia1.rates_of(o, n, s.n_trials, bw)) for o in shifted]
        info_sh[(s.name, bw)] = {m: {k: np.mean([x[m][k] for x in sh]) for k in sh[0][m]} for m in sh[0]}


def fit_rows(sel, bw, src):
    rows = []
    for s in sel:
        inf = src[(s.name, bw)]
        ns = np.array(sorted(inf))
        i1 = np.array([inf[n]["i1"] for n in ns])
        rbar = np.array([inf[n]["rbar"] for n in ns])
        rate = np.array([inf[n]["rate"] for n in ns])
        occ = rbar / rbar.sum()
        row = dict(session=s.name, kept_c=s.name in POP["c"], protocol=s.protocol, n_max=ns.max(), n_values=len(ns))
        for name, y in [("i1", i1), ("i1_ii", i1 * T), ("occ_log2", np.log2(occ)), ("occ_ln", np.log(occ)),
                        ("occ_log10", np.log10(occ)), ("rate", rate)]:
            sl, se, pg, p2 = ia1.line_fit(ns, y)
            row.update({f"{name}_slope": sl, f"{name}_se": se, f"{name}_pg": pg, f"{name}_p2": p2})
        row["total_rate"] = rate.sum()
        row["frac_gt1"] = rate[ns > 1].sum() / rate.sum()
        rows.append(row)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

fig7ab-information-per-burst-increases¶

The information carried by each n-burst increases with n; every bursting session has a significantly positive slope of I_n(1) against n, with an average slope of 1.5 bits (SD 0.7 bits) over 59 bursting cells.

Significance (a) slope more than one standard error above zero, (b) one-sided t-test p < 0.05. Sessions with fewer than three n values have no error for the slope and count as not significant.

Result: partially reproduced. Over the 64 bursting sessions of selection (c), within 59 +/- 5.9, the mean slope of I_n(1) on n is 2.22 bits (SD 0.87) with 0.1 ms bins, just outside 1.5 +/- 0.7, and 1.91 (SD 0.75) with 0.4 ms bins in bits per event, 1.78 and 1.53 for Eq. 10 as printed, within. All 64 slopes are positive; 63 are significant by one standard error and 62 by the t-test (one session has only two n values), so not every session. Over the 84 bursting sessions of selection (a), outside 59 +/- 5.9, the slopes are 2.14, 1.85, 1.71 and 1.48.

The baseline with each trial's burst onsets shifted at random gives a larger mean slope, 2.59 bits with 0.1 ms bins and 2.23 with 0.4 ms bins (selection (c)); the slope of the data exceeds that of its shifted copy in only 3 of 64 sessions (9 with 0.4 ms bins). A shifted train has lost its locking to the stimulus, so its rate is spread over more bins and its plug-in bias is at least that of the data; the comparison shows that the bias of the estimate for rare events is of the order of the rise of I_n(1) with n, not that the whole rise is bias. The criterion fixes the formula, so the outcome rests on it.

fig7ef-jitter-independent-of-n¶

The jitter of the first spike of a burst is roughly independent of n in 80% of the bursting sessions, and the mean slope of jitter against n is -0.03 ms (SD 0.2 ms).

Jitter per n is the mean over events of the SD of the onset times. Events (a) peaks of the onset histogram in 0.1 ms bins, between the troughs on either side; (b) onsets within the session's first-peak domain (the limiting ISI) centred on an event centre, the centres being the histogram bins taken from the highest down (ia1.jitter_events_b). Slopes over the n values with a jitter (events with at least two onsets); "not significant" is (a) |slope| below one standard error, (b) two-sided p >= 0.05; sessions with fewer than three such n values have no test and are counted apart.

In [19]:

direct-method-comparison¶

Information rates from the burst code are highly correlated with those of the direct method (R = 0.95), averaging 191 against 222 bits/s, the direct method being higher in all sessions but one by 31 bits/s on average, so the burst code keeps about 85% of the information.

Direct method on binary words of 0.4 ms bins, words starting at every bin over 200 to 1000 ms, entropies NSB-corrected (ia1.nsb_entropy). Readings (a) the rate at 8 bins (3.2 ms), (b) a linear extrapolation in 1 / word length over 1 to 8 bins. The burst-code rate is I' of fig7gh (non-bursting sessions as all 1-bursts), with bins (a) 0.1 ms and (b) 0.4 ms. Sessions (a) all kept, (b) bursting.

The direct method is higher in 74 of 89 sessions (83%), not in all but one. Over the bursting sessions R = 0.951, 220.7 against 199.8 bits/s, difference 21.0, higher in 52 of 64. Over selection (a) the values are alike (R = 0.965, 204.3 against 183.6, 10.1% lost, 94 of 115). The extrapolated direct rate changes these by under 1 bit/s. With 0.1 ms bins the burst code is above the direct method on average (220.1 against 198.4 bits/s).

Burst-triggered averages: per-session measures¶

For each bursting session (main reading), the stimulus in dB (stimulus file shifted to the intensity in cell.dat, as stimtodB.m does) around every burst onset in 200 to 1000 ms, from -25 to +15 ms at 20 kHz (Methods, Estimation of burst-triggered averages). tau_n is the distance from the nBTA's central maximum to the onset (Eq. 13 and the sentence after it: "The time tau_n between the maximum of nBTA and tau = 0"), which the Results call "the mean delay between stimulus upstroke and burst generation" (Qualitative description, paragraph 3). The central maximum is therefore searched (a) before the onset, -25 to 0 ms, the main reading since revision 1; (b) over the whole window, -25 to +15 ms, the reading of the first round, shown as a variant.

A session enters the analyses of n = 1 to 4 when it has at least two bursts of each n, the least that gives a variance; the paper says only that eight sessions had "too few bursts" (Results, paragraph 6), so this is an assumption, and the results with at least 20 and at least 50 bursts of each n are shown too.

In [22]:
def p_two_sided_ttests(a, b):
    return stats.ttest_ind(a, b, axis=0).pvalue


SEARCH = {"a": (-ia1.PRE, 0.0), "b": None}       # where the central maximum is searched

BTA = {}
for s in BURSTING_A:
    st = stim_db(s)
    tr, on, n = ia1.bursts(s.trials, LIM[s.name])
    seg = {}
    for m in range(1, 5):
        if (n == m).sum() >= 2:
            seg[m], tt = ia1.segments(st, on[n == m])
    sp = spikes_in(s)
    sta_seg, tt = ia1.segments(st, sp)
    BTA[s.name] = dict(seg=seg, tt=tt, sta_seg=sta_seg, on=on, n=n, tr=tr, mean_stim=st[4000:20000].mean(),
                       counts=[len(seg[m]) if m in seg else int((n == m).sum()) for m in range(1, 5)])
have4 = [s for s in BURSTING_A if len(BTA[s.name]["seg"]) == 4]
for kr in "ca":
    bs = [s for s in BURSTING_A if s.name in POP[kr]]
    print(f"kept ({kr}): bursting sessions {len(bs)}; with at least k bursts of each n = 1 to 4:",
          {k: sum(min(BTA[s.name]["counts"]) >= k for s in bs) for k in MIN_BURSTS})
cnt4 = np.array([BTA[s.name]["counts"][3] for s in have4 if s.name in POP["c"]])
print("kept (c), sessions with n = 1 to 4: number of 4-bursts, quantiles 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1:", np.quantile(cnt4, [0, .25, .5, .75, 1]))


def subset(rows_df, kr, k):
    # Rows of sessions in selection kr with at least k bursts of each n = 1 to 4.
    ok = {s.name for s in have4 if s.name in POP[kr] and min(BTA[s.name]["counts"]) >= k}
    return rows_df[rows_df.session.isin(ok)]

fig8-nbta-differ¶

In every bursting cell the burst-triggered averages for n = 1 to 4 differ significantly (in the example cell their central peaks grow higher and wider with n); 50 of the 58 bursting sessions show significantly different central peaks in the time domain, the other eight having too few bursts.

Two-way ANOVAs (frequency bin x n) on the real and the imaginary parts of the Fourier transform of each segment, each at 0.01 / 2; frequency bins (a) all, (b) up to the cutoff. Then at each time point, t-tests of each nBTA against the three others, p < 0.01; a point is marked for n when all three are significant. Central peak: from the minimum before to the minimum after the central maximum, searched (a) before the onset or (b) over the whole window. Readings (a) at least one marked point in the central peak of every n, (b) more than half of the points of every central peak marked. The two-way ANOVAs treat every segment and frequency bin as an observation, as the Methods describe; with hundreds to thousands of segments they reject in nearly every session.

rows = []
for s in have4:
    B = BTA[s.name]
    tt = B["tt"]
    segs = [B["seg"][m] for m in range(1, 5)]
    ffts = [np.fft.rfft(g, axis=1) for g in segs]
    freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(tt), 1 / ia1.STIM_RATE)
    row = dict(session=s.name, protocol=s.protocol, counts=[len(g) for g in segs])
    for fr, sel in [("a", slice(None)), ("b", freqs <= s.cutoff)]:
        ps = []
        for part in [np.real, np.imag]:
            gs = [part(f)[:, sel] for f in ffts]
            if part is np.imag:
                gs = [g[:, 1:] for g in gs]          # the imaginary part of the 0 Hz bin is 0
            ps.append(min(ia1.two_way_anova(gs)))
        row[f"anova_{fr}"] = min(ps) < 0.01 / 2
    btas = [g.mean(0) for g in segs]
    sig = []
    for i in range(4):
        x = np.ones(len(tt), bool)
        for j in range(4):
            if j != i:
                x &= p_two_sided_ttests(segs[i], segs[j]) < 0.01
        sig.append(x)
    for sr in "ab":
        marked = []
        for i in range(4):
            ip, a, b = ia1.central_peak(btas[i], tt, SEARCH[sr])
            marked.append(sig[i][a:b + 1].mean())
        row[f"peak_any_{sr}"] = all(m > 0 for m in marked)
        row[f"peak_most_{sr}"] = all(m > 0.5 for m in marked)
        row[f"marked_{sr}"] = [round(m, 2) for m in marked]
    rows.append(row)
N8 = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(subset(N8, "c", 2).to_string(index=False))
out = []
for kr, k, sr in itertools.product("ca", MIN_BURSTS, "ab"):
    g = subset(N8, kr, k)
    out.append(dict(kept=kr, min_bursts=k, search=sr, sessions=len(g), bursting=sum(s.name in POP[kr] for s in BURSTING_A),
                    anova_a=int(g.anova_a.sum()), anova_b=int(g.anova_b.sum()),
                    peak_any=int((g.anova_a & g[f"peak_any_{sr}"]).sum()), peak_most=int((g.anova_a & g[f"peak_most_{sr}"]).sum())))
print()
print(pd.DataFrame(out).to_string(index=False))

Result: partially reproduced. Of the 64 bursting sessions of selection (c) (58 +/- 5.8 in the paper, so just outside), 53 have at least two bursts of each n = 1 to 4, and all 53 pass the frequency-domain ANOVA, with all frequency bins and with bins up to the cutoff. In the time domain, with the central maximum searched before the onset (main reading), 38 of them have marked points in every central peak (reading a), outside 50 +/- 5, and 5 have most of every central peak marked (reading b); with the maximum searched over the whole window, 42 and 7. With at least 20 bursts of each n, 39 sessions, 33 and 35; with at least 50, 28 sessions, 25 and 26. Over selection (a), 71 sessions all pass the ANOVA and 54 (60 over the whole window) have marked points in every central peak. The ANOVA part of the claim holds; the time-domain count does not.

fig8-latency-decreases¶

The latency between the stimulus upstroke and burst onset decreases with n, so that high or wide deflections produce prompt responses with high-n bursts.

tau_n per session with bursts of n = 1 to 4. Readings (a) tau_n decreasing from n = 1 to 4 (tau_4 < tau_1 with no increase between consecutive n) in the majority of those sessions; (b) the mean over sessions of tau_n decreasing from 1 to 4.

rows = []
for s in have4:
    B = BTA[s.name]
    row = dict(session=s.name, protocol=s.protocol)
    for sr in "ab":
        taus = [-B["tt"][ia1.central_peak(B["seg"][m].mean(0), B["tt"], SEARCH[sr])[0]] * 1e3 for m in range(1, 5)]
        row.update({f"tau{m}_{sr}": t for m, t in zip(range(1, 5), taus)})
        row[f"decreasing_{sr}"] = all(np.diff(taus) <= 0) and taus[3] < taus[0]
        row[f"tau4_below_tau1_{sr}"] = taus[3] < taus[0]
    rows.append(row)
LT = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(subset(LT, "c", 2).round(2).to_string(index=False))
out = []
for kr, k, sr in itertools.product("ca", MIN_BURSTS, "ab"):
    g = subset(LT, kr, k)
    tau = g[[f"tau{m}_{sr}" for m in range(1, 5)]]
    out.append(dict(kept=kr, min_bursts=k, search=sr, sessions=len(g), decreasing=int(g[f"decreasing_{sr}"].sum()),
                    tau4_below_tau1=int(g[f"tau4_below_tau1_{sr}"].sum()), mean_tau_ms=tau.mean().round(2).tolist(),
                    negative_tau=int((tau.values < 0).any(axis=1).sum()),
                    wilcoxon_p=stats.wilcoxon(g[f"tau1_{sr}"], g[f"tau4_{sr}"]).pvalue if len(g) > 5 else np.nan))
print()
print(pd.DataFrame(out).to_string(index=False))
# The search before the onset ends at 0 ms, so a maximum found there sits on the edge of the search.
print()
for kr in "ca":
    g = subset(LT, kr, 2)
    tau = g[[f"tau{m}_a" for m in range(1, 5)]].values
    edge = np.isclose(tau, 0)
    free, free3 = ~edge.any(axis=1), ~edge[:, :3].any(axis=1)
    print(f"kept ({kr}), search before onset: sessions with a tau_n at the 0 ms edge", int(edge.any(axis=1).sum()), "of", len(g),
          "; values at the edge", int(edge.sum()), "(per n", edge.sum(0).tolist(), ")")
    print("  sessions with no tau_n at the edge:", int(free.sum()), "; their mean tau_n", tau[free].mean(0).round(2).tolist(),
          "; decreasing at every step", int(g.decreasing_a.values[free].sum()), "; tau_4 < tau_1", int(g.tau4_below_tau1_a.values[free].sum()))
    dec3 = (tau[:, 0] > tau[:, 1]) & (tau[:, 1] > tau[:, 2])
    print("  sessions with tau_1 to tau_3 off the edge:", int(free3.sum()), "; tau_1 > tau_2 > tau_3 in", int(dec3[free3].sum()),
          "; tau_3 < tau_1 in", int((tau[:, 2] < tau[:, 0])[free3].sum()))
    print("  mean tau_n with the values at the edge left out:", [round(tau[~edge[:, m], m].mean(), 2) for m in range(4)])

Result: reproduced (reading b). With the central maximum searched before the burst onset, the mean latency over the 53 sessions of selection (c) falls with n: 5.80, 4.23, 3.32 and 2.67 ms for n = 1 to 4; no tau_n is negative, which holds by construction as the search ends at 0 ms. In 13 of the 53 sessions 17 values of tau_n sit on that edge (1 for n = 2, 5 for n = 3, 11 for n = 4), and the mean tau_4 includes them. Leaving those values out, the means are 5.80, 4.32, 3.67 and 3.37 ms, still falling; over the 40 sessions with no value on the edge they are 5.77, 4.33, 3.77 and 3.40 ms, and of the 48 sessions with tau_1 to tau_3 off the edge, 32 have tau_1 > tau_2 > tau_3. 51 of 53 sessions have tau_4 < tau_1 (Wilcoxon p = 4.5e-9), but only 20 of 53 decrease at every step (reading a, not a majority). With the maximum searched over the whole window, as in the first round, the means are 5.80, 4.22, 3.14 and -0.50 ms, with a negative tau_n in 33 sessions, where the 4BTA peaks after the onset. With at least 20 or 50 bursts of each n the means also fall (6.01 to 2.12 and 5.88 to 2.05 ms), and over selection (a) they fall from 5.75 to 2.46 ms.

fig8e-sigma-minimum¶

The standard deviation of the stimuli preceding an n-burst has a minimum at a position nearly the same for all n; over the bursting cells the SD of the minimum's position across n = 1 to 4 averages 0.4 ms (SD 0.7 ms), roughly 0.05 times the inverse cutoff frequency.

sigma_n(tau) by Eq. 14. Window for the minimum (a) -25 to 0 ms, (b) -25 to +15 ms. The SD across the four n is the sample SD (N - 1), as MATLAB's std; the population SD (N) is shown too. With few segments sigma_n is noisy and its minimum wanders, so the result is shown for sessions with at least 2, 20 and 50 bursts of each n.

The minimum of sigma_n lies near -6 ms for every n (medians -6.85, -6.3, -4.8 and -6.6 ms over the 53 sessions of selection (c)), but the SD of its position across n = 1 to 4 averages 2.37 ms (SD 2.44) in window (a) and 2.84 ms in window (b), outside 0.4 +/- 0.7, and 2.05 and 2.46 ms with the population SD; times the cutoff it is 0.35 to 0.48, against 0.05. Requiring more bursts of each n narrows it but not to the paper's value: 2.14 ms with at least 20 (39 sessions) and 1.74 ms with at least 50 (28 sessions; 0.19 times the cutoff), and 1.46 ms over the 38 such sessions of selection (a).

sigma-n-below-sta-sigma¶

In 98% of bursting cells, for all n, the SD of the stimuli preceding an n-burst is smaller than the SD of the stimuli preceding all spikes, by a ratio of minima of 1.62 on average (SD 0.56).

"Smaller" read as (a) the minimum of sigma_n below the minimum of sigma, (b) sigma_n below sigma at every tau in -25 to +15 ms; n = 1 to 4. The ratio is min sigma over the mean over n of min sigma_n, minima over -25 to +15 ms (and over -25 to 0 ms as a variant).

The minimum over 800 time points of an SD estimated from few segments is biased low, so a smaller minimum for the n-bursts could come from their smaller number alone. As a control (not in the paper), sigma is also computed from random subsets of the segments preceding all spikes, of the same size as each n's, 20 draws per n, and the minimum of sigma_n is compared with the mean minimum of these size-matched sigmas.

Result: reproduced. In 98.1% of the 53 sessions of selection (c) the minimum of sigma_n is below the minimum of sigma for all n = 1 to 4 (reading a), within 98 +/- 9.8, and the ratio of the minima averages 1.596 (SD 0.280), within 1.62 +/- 0.56. Read as sigma_n below sigma at every tau (b), it holds in 1.9%. The result is not an effect of the smaller number of n-bursts: sigma from random subsets of the spike-triggered segments of the same size has a minimum about 5% below that of all segments (0.5 to 0.8% with at least 20 or 50 bursts of each n), the minimum of sigma_n is below that size-matched minimum for every n in 94.3% of sessions, and the ratio to it is 1.517. With at least 20 or 50 bursts of each n the values are 97.4% and 1.562, and 96.4% and 1.571. The ratios per n are 1.27, 1.45 and 1.62 for n = 1 to 3; for n = 4 the mean is 23.5, inflated by sessions with few 4-bursts, and 2.38 with at least 20.

fig9-nbta-not-concatenated-1bta¶

The nBTA differs from n 1BTAs shifted by the burst's own ISIs and summed; for a large fraction of cells the difference is significant, the fraction diminishing as n grows; results are similar with shifted STAs.

f_n(t) = sum over the burst's spikes of 1BTA(t - t_i) (Eq. 15). Summing n copies of a stimulus in dB only compares with the nBTA once the mean stimulus is subtracted (as the paper does for Figure 9C); this is taken as the reading of Eq. 15, an assumption, and the average of the shifted copies (the sum over n) is shown as a variant. The 1BTA (or STA) is computed from -60 to +15 ms so that its shifts cover the window. Comparison over the interval between the minima flanking the central maximum of the nBTA (searched before the onset): two-way ANOVAs (frequency bin x group) on the real and imaginary parts of the Fourier transform, at 0.01 / 2, with observations (a) each burst's segment against its own f_n (paired: ANOVA on the differences), (b) the segments and the f_n as two groups. Then t-tests at each time point (p < 0.01) and sessions with more than 70% of the interval significant.

In [27]:
def paired_anova(d):
    # Differences segment - f_n per burst (rows) and frequency bin (columns): p of a mean
    # difference (group main effect) and of its variation across bins (the interaction).
    Nb, F = d.shape
    m = d.mean()
    mf = d.mean(0)
    ss_err = ((d - mf) ** 2).sum()
    df_err = (Nb - 1) * F
    ms = ss_err / df_err
    p_main = stats.f.sf(Nb * F * m ** 2 / ms, 1, df_err)
    p_int = stats.f.sf(Nb * ((mf - m) ** 2).sum() / (F - 1) / ms, F - 1, df_err)
    return min(p_main, p_int)


rows = []
for s in BURSTING_A:
    B = BTA[s.name]
    st = stim_db(s)
    ms = B["mean_stim"]
    tr, on, n = B["tr"], B["on"], B["n"]
    long_t0 = 0.06
    one, tl = ia1.segments(st, on[n == 1], pre=long_t0)
    allsp, _ = ia1.segments(st, spikes_in(s), pre=long_t0)
    kernels = {"1BTA": one.mean(0) - ms, "STA": allsp.mean(0) - ms}
    i_zero = int(round(long_t0 * ia1.STIM_RATE))
    for m in [2, 3, 4]:
        if m not in B["seg"]:
            continue
        idx = np.flatnonzero(n == m)
        seg = B["seg"][m] - ms
        tt = B["tt"]
        ip, a, b = ia1.central_peak(seg.mean(0), tt, SEARCH["a"])
        if b - a < 3:
            continue
        # spike offsets of each burst relative to its onset
        trial_spikes = s.trials
        for kname, ker in kernels.items():
            for scale in ["sum", "mean"]:
                fn = np.zeros_like(seg)
                for r, k in enumerate(idx):
                    t = trial_spikes[tr[k]]
                    j = np.searchsorted(t, on[k])
                    offs = t[j:j + m] - on[k]
                    for o in offs:
                        sh = int(round(o * ia1.STIM_RATE))
                        fn[r] += ker[i_zero - 500 - sh:i_zero + 300 - sh]
                    if scale == "mean":
                        fn[r] /= m
                x, y = seg[:, a:b + 1], fn[:, a:b + 1]
                X, Y = np.fft.rfft(x, axis=1), np.fft.rfft(y, axis=1)
                pa = min(paired_anova(np.real(X - Y)), paired_anova(np.imag(X - Y)[:, 1:]) if X.shape[1] > 2 else 1)
                pb = min(min(ia1.two_way_anova([np.real(X), np.real(Y)])), min(ia1.two_way_anova([np.imag(X)[:, 1:], np.imag(Y)[:, 1:]])) if X.shape[1] > 2 else 1)
                tp = stats.ttest_ind(x, y, axis=0).pvalue
                rows.append(dict(session=s.name, kept_c=s.name in POP["c"], n=m, kernel=kname, scale=scale, bursts=len(idx), anova_a=pa < 0.005, anova_b=pb < 0.005,
                                 t_frac=(tp < 0.01).mean()))
N9 = pd.DataFrame(rows)
summ = []
for (kname, scale, m), g0 in N9.groupby(["kernel", "scale", "n"]):
    for kr, g in [("c", g0[g0.kept_c]), ("a", g0)]:
        summ.append(dict(kept=kr, kernel=kname, scale=scale, n=m, sessions=len(g), anova_a_pct=round(100 * g.anova_a.mean(), 1),
                         anova_b_pct=round(100 * g.anova_b.mean(), 1),
                         t70_a_pct=round(100 * (g.anova_a & (g.t_frac > 0.7)).mean(), 1),
                         t70_b_pct=round(100 * (g.anova_b & (g.t_frac > 0.7)).mean(), 1)))

Result: reproduced (resting on subtracting the mean stimulus before summing the 1BTAs). Over the bursting sessions of selection (c) the nBTA differs from the summed 1BTAs by the ANOVA in 100% of the sessions for n = 2, 3 and 4 with paired observations (a), and in 100%, 100% and 98.1% with grouped ones (b), so the fraction does not grow with n; the share with more than 70% of the interval significant falls from 93.8% (n = 2) to 84.1% and 52.8% (n = 4). With the STA the ANOVA fractions are 100%, 100% and 98.1% (a) and the 70% share falls from 100% to 37.7%; with the average of the shifted copies in place of their sum the results are alike, and so are those over selection (a). An ANOVA that rejects in nearly every session separates little; the criterion specifies it.

fig9c-population-nbta¶

In the seven cells driven at 100 Hz cutoff and 6 dB, the population-average nBTAs show that bursts with more spikes follow higher or wider stimulus deflections, with large spread across cells.

Each session's 1BTA, 2BTA and 3BTA minus its mean stimulus, shifted so that its central maximum sits at the mean tau_n over the sessions (shifting by tau_n, averaging and shifting back), averaged over the bursting protocol-5 sessions with at least two bursts of n = 1 to 3. Width (a) full width at half height, (b) between the minima flanking the central maximum. The central maximum is searched before the onset and, as a variant, over the whole window.

fig10-burst-n-vs-height¶

The probability of a burst with n spikes after a stimulus maximum depends on its height, low excursions giving no response or an isolated spike and high ones doublets, triplets or 4-bursts; all bursting cells show this.

Methods (Relating burst probabilities to the height of stimulus excursions), per trial: each n-burst shifted back by tau_n (the maximum of the nBTA searched (a) before the onset, (b) over the whole window); each local maximum of the stimulus in 200 to 1000 ms matched to the burst whose shifted onset is closest within [t0 - T, t0 + T]; a burst matched to more than one maximum kept by the nearest, the other maxima counting as no response. T is the width of the central STA peak, (a) between its flanking minima, (b) full width at half height. P(n | h) in windows of half-width 5% of the span of h, at 41 centres. Segregation (a) the h at which P(n | h) peaks increases with n for n = 0 to the largest n with bursts (up to 4); (b) the mean of h weighted by P(n | h) increases with n. Bursting sessions with bursts of n = 1 and 2 at least.

from scipy.signal import argrelmax


def p_n_given_h(s, Twin, sr):
    B = BTA[s.name]
    st = stim_db(s)
    i0, i1 = int(ia1.T0 * ia1.STIM_RATE), int(ia1.T1 * ia1.STIM_RATE)
    mx = argrelmax(st[i0:i1])[0] + i0
    tmax, h = mx / ia1.STIM_RATE, st[mx]
    tt = B["tt"]
    tau = {m: -tt[ia1.central_peak(B["seg"][m].mean(0), tt, SEARCH[sr])[0]] for m in B["seg"]}
    resp = []
    for i in range(s.n_trials):
        k = B["tr"] == i
        on, n = B["on"][k], B["n"][k]
        sh = on - np.array([tau.get(m, tau[max(tau)]) for m in n])
        best = np.full(len(tmax), -1)
        for j, t0 in enumerate(tmax):
            d = np.abs(sh - t0)
            if len(d) and d.min() <= Twin:
                best[j] = np.argmin(d)
        r = np.zeros(len(tmax), int)
        for bi in np.unique(best[best >= 0]):
            js = np.flatnonzero(best == bi)
            jbest = js[np.argmin(np.abs(tmax[js] - sh[bi]))]
            r[jbest] = n[bi]
        resp.append(r)
    resp = np.concatenate(resp)
    matched = int((resp > 0).sum())
    hh = np.tile(h, s.n_trials)
    span = hh.max() - hh.min()
    centres = np.linspace(hh.min(), hh.max(), 41)
    nmax = min(4, resp.max())
    P = np.array([[np.mean(resp[np.abs(hh - c) <= 0.05 * span] == m) if (np.abs(hh - c) <= 0.05 * span).any() else np.nan
                   for c in centres] for m in range(nmax + 1)])
    occupancy = np.array([(np.abs(hh - c) <= 0.05 * span).sum() for c in centres])
    return centres, P, nmax, matched, np.bincount(np.minimum(resp, 4), minlength=5), occupancy


rows = []
example = None
for s, sr in itertools.product(BURSTING_A, "ab"):
    B = BTA[s.name]
    if not (1 in B["seg"] and 2 in B["seg"]):
        continue
    tt = B["tt"]
    sta = B["sta_seg"].mean(0) - B["mean_stim"]
    ip, a, b = ia1.central_peak(sta, tt, SEARCH[sr])
    for tw, Tw in [("a", (b - a) / ia1.STIM_RATE), ("b", ia1.fwhm(sta, ip, 0.0) / ia1.STIM_RATE)]:

Result: not reproduced. Over the 64 bursting sessions of selection (c), with each n-burst shifted back by tau_n found before the onset, the h at which P(n | h) peaks increases from n = 0 to the largest n (up to 4) in 7 sessions (10.9%) and the P-weighted mean h in 15 (23.4%), under both widths T, against all bursting cells. With tau_n searched over the whole window the counts are 7 and 16, and over selection (a) 8 and 19 to 21 of 84. Restricted to n = 0 to 3, a variant outside the criterion, the ordering holds in 34 and 36 to 37 of 64 sessions: the 4-bursts, which are few, most often break it. The two T readings match a different number of maxima in 58 of 64 sessions (a median of 8316 against 8173), yet the peak flag changes in none and the mean flag in 2, one each way: the peak of P(n | h) on the 41-point grid of h does not move when about 2% of the matches change, which is why the counts are equal.

firing-rate-no-effect-on-limit¶

The firing rate has practically no effect on the limiting ISI; a 50 Hz increase in rate shifts it by less than 0.4 ms and raises the average n by less than 25%.

Reading (a), the same cell and stimulus at two target rates 50 Hz apart: the headers record target rates of 100 and 90 Hz only (Data check), so no pair exists. Reading (b): linear regressions over the kept sessions of the limiting ISI (bursting sessions) and of the average n on the session's rate, scaled to 50 Hz; the increase of the average n is relative to its mean.

Result: reproduced (reading b). No cell was recorded at two target rates (the headers hold 100 and 90 Hz only), so reading (a) cannot be formed. Across the sessions of selection (c) a 50 Hz higher rate goes with a limiting ISI shorter by 0.337 ms (p = 0.44, 64 bursting sessions), below 0.44 ms, and an average n higher by 15.7% (p = 0.132, 89 sessions), below 27.5%; within protocol 1 alone, 0.057 ms and 18.9%. Over selection (a), 0.189 ms and 13.6%. These are differences between cells, not the within-cell change the paper may have measured.

model-reproduces-coding-trends (blocked)¶

The threshold-linear model with refractoriness reproduces the coding trends of the data, at single-cell and population level, though it is less precise in time than the real cells.

Depends on model-matches-classification, which is blocked (data_missing, no thresholds s_TH).

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's:

  • Population. The paper keeps 86 of its 132 sessions by the rate SD (< 35 Hz) and a rate near 100 Hz. In the data set that rule keeps 115 of the 116 sessions of the paper's seven protocols. Leaving out also the 9 sessions with fewer than 98 trials (the paper gives 98 to 503) and the sessions sorted off-line (selection c) keeps 89, with 47, 6, 7, 7, 8, 7 and 7 per protocol against the paper's 43, 6, 7, 7, 8, 7 and 8, and bursting sessions per protocol equal to Table 1's in six of seven, but from 29 cells on 18 dates. Selection (c) is the main population from firing-rate-uniform on, an assumption: the off-line exclusion has no passage in the paper behind it, and as it was chosen in part from Table 1's counts it is only a variant for the claims on those counts. The results over the 115 sessions of selection (a), the population of the first round, are shown beside it.
  • Burst identification. The Methods leave open which maximum is the first peak, which minimum bounds it and what sigma and N are in the error bar. The first local maximum (peak reading a) falls on edge effects of the refractory plateau, where C_s has no spike pairs, and leaves 11 of 89 sessions bursting; started after the plateau (peak reading c) it gives 61, close to the 64 of the main reading. With N the number of trials the error bars are so wide that no session bursts. The main reading is the largest value below 5 ms, the first significant minimum after it, and N the number of product terms, under which the error bar is 2.6% of the span of C_s (the paper's 3.4%). Outcomes that rest on bursts are marked as resting on this choice.
  • Burst-triggered averages. The central maximum of an nBTA, which gives tau_n, is searched before the burst onset (the paper calls tau_n the delay between stimulus upstroke and burst generation); the first round searched the whole window, which put the 4BTA's maximum after the onset in many sessions. Sessions need at least two bursts of each n; results with at least 20 and 50 are shown.
  • Information. I_n(1) and I'_n are plug-in estimates, as the criterion gives them. A baseline with each trial's burst onsets shifted at random gives a larger rise of I_n(1) with n than the data, so the bias of the estimate is of the order of that rise.
  • Thresholds. The data set holds no threshold s_TH, so the model of Eq. 2 and the claims on it are blocked.
  • Smaller choices are stated in each section: the stimulus is the AM signal in dB from stimtodB.m with the intensity of cell.dat; f_n of Eq. 15 sums 1BTAs after subtracting the mean stimulus; peaks of C_s are counted with a prominence threshold.

What was found about the dataset:

  • Data1 holds 150 sessions (75 experiments of two stimuli each) of 45 cells; 116 sessions from 37 cells on 23 dates use the paper's seven protocols, the paper's 37 cells; 28 sessions use the gaussModality and lmd stimuli and 6 use cutoffs of 50 and 1600 Hz, which the paper does not mention. Nothing marks the 86 sessions the paper kept.
  • Data1 records no animal, no threshold and no best frequency; cell.dat gives the intensity played. 28 sessions were sorted off-line and have no header; in 25 of them the trial blocks run on into the pause (spikes up to 2.76 s, at a median 2.7 Hz from 1 to 1.7 s), while no on-line block goes past 1.02 s. Each block is one trial: none is sorted out of order or holds twice the usual spike count. firing_rates gives each spike file's trial count, which matches the blocks parsed here in 136 of 138 files, and a rate whose +/- value (median 128 Hz) is not the trial-to-trial SD (median 5.8 Hz).
  • The intensity in three headers differs from cell.dat by more than 1 dB (up to 6.6 dB); the descriptor says 98 to 533 trials, the files hold 69 to 503; six sessions had pauses of 450 ms, not 700. Two experiments (03-01-15-aa, 03-06-27-ae) are missing from singlecells.txt.
  • Spikes and stimuli share the trial clock: the STA peaks 5.6 ms (median) before the spike, at 0 ms in one session (03-03-06-aa sig2), exceeds the STA with the stimulus shifted by 100 ms in all 116 sessions, and almost vanishes with the stimulus shifted by 100 ms.
